title: ‘Worst own goal’: No Labor modelling of SMSF property ban
full_text:
Labor did not model how housing supply would be impacted by banning self-managed superannuation funds from borrowing to buy property, prompting an industry economist to label the policy the “worst own goal in this year’s budget”.
A Coalition freedom of information request to obtain the regulatory impact statement of the SMSF policy was rejected as “Treasury holds no documents within the scope of your request”.
“No documents were located as a regulatory impact statement was not required to be prepared,” a Treasury official wrote in a letter to opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg.
Labor agreed to ban SMSF borrowing to purchase new homes to strike a deal with the Greens to ram negative gearing and capital gains tax reforms through parliament ahead of parliament’s winter break in July.
Jim Chalmers said at the time the reform would have little impact on the housing market, but industry groups are warning it will have a stark impact to supply and push the target of 1.2 million new homes further out of reach.
Housing Industry Association chief economist Tim Reardon said “we’ve known for a long time self-managed super funds were an important component to new home building”.
“About 45 per cent of new homes built in Australia are financed by small and medium-sized businesses, and we know that SMSFs are categorised as small and medium-sized businesses,” Mr Reardon said.
“This is the worst own goal in this year’s budget. There is no evidence of a benefit but there is very clear evidence in a reduction of supply.
“They provided in the budget, in the budget, estimates of the increase in rents and the reduction in home building as a consequence of negative gearing and the capital gains tax.
“But there has been no public effort to demonstrate a public benefit as a result of the prohibition on self-managed super funds.”
Senator Bragg accused the Albanese government of deliberately reducing housing supply.
“Labor kicked SMSFs out of housing because they didn’t like the investors. But they did so without even doing the basic work. Treasury has now confirmed there was no regulatory impact statement before these changes were rammed through,” Senator Bragg said.
“Had Labor bothered to do the regulatory impact analysis, they would have understood that SMSF investors cannot live in these properties. They are simply properties which add to housing and rental supply.
“In many cases, these are off-the-plan developments, which may now be in doubt due to the ban.
“This is inconsistent with Labor’s primary housing tax hikes, which distinguish between new and existing homes.”
Labor's Treasury Amendment laws, first announced on Budget night, passed through the Senate on Thursday afternoon. These laws were expected to pass through the Upper House this week, after Labor reached a deal with the Greens. The amendments have been described as the biggest change to taxation in a generation, affecting capital gains tax, negative gearing of properties, and trusts. The Greens agreed to help pass the laws in exchange for an eight-week extension to the inquiry into NDIS eligibility, and a new clause in the legislation to prevent self-managed super funds from borrowing money to buy residential properties.
A spokesman for the Treasurer leapt on the timing of the FOI refusal, which was provided to Senator Bragg in July.
“Multiple inquiries have raised concerns that these arrangements raise risks for superannuation investors, including the 2014 Murray Financial System Inquiry conducted for the Coalition,” the spokesman said.
“Senator Bragg is trotting out a document he was provided more than a month ago to distract from the fact he wants to cut housing and attack the superannuation system.”
A recent HIA survey showed builders reported more than 3600 SMSF-funded homes were yet to be built, with 70 per cent of them expected to be cancelled.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has agreed to a deal with the Greens to ban self-managed super funds from borrowing money to purchase properties for investment in exchange for support on Labor’s tax reforms. “When it comes to the physical impact, we anticipate something like a $50 million positive impact,” Mr Chalmers said. “We have supported different versions of this in the past; we took seriously the recommendation from David Murray.”
A survey of Australian Finance Industry Association members showed more than 16,000 new residential SMSF loans were written in the year to June 2026, far higher than the 4000 claim from the government.
“As AFIA members do not represent the full market, the true figure is likely higher,” the body said in a July statement.
With budget tax changes contributing to national house price declines, Reserve Bank of Australia chief economist Sarah Hunter last week said the impact on supply would be felt later in the year.
“(Interest rate rises, tax changes, and the war in the Middle East are) going to have an impact on new dwelling supply in the future, which is, as I said, that’s why we’ve got a new dwelling supply profile that has activity dropping down, at the end of the forecast horizon,” she said last week.
